Reservoir sampling

Source: R/design-reservoir.R
design_reservoir.Rd

Draws a uniform sample of fixed size from a stream of unknown length in a single pass, using Algorithm L (Li 1994), which skips ahead geometrically instead of drawing a random number for every item (Vitter 1985).

Usage

design_reservoir(n, max_items = Inf, batches = FALSE)

Arguments

n

Reservoir size, or a plan from plan_size(). Fewer items come back if the stream is shorter; the result is never padded.

max_items

Stop after this many items, or rows with batches = TRUE. Items past the cap are never sampled, so inclusion_prob() gives rows past it 0 and gives the rows before it n / max_items rather than n / N. A stream is read one item past the cap; see "What is read". Inf reads the whole stream. Warns when the cap truncates.

batches

If TRUE, data is a function that returns a data frame of rows on each call and NULL at the end, and the reservoir samples rows rather than whole data frames. draw() then returns a data frame. A data frame given as data is sampled by rows either way; a list or a connection is refused.

Value

A design object, for use with draw().

Details

A data frame or a list is not a stream: its length is already known and it already fits in memory, so draw() picks n positions in it at random and returns them in their original order. Every element of a list is an item, NULL included, and the elements keep their names. The streaming path is for data that does not fit in memory. Pass it a connection, or a function that returns the next item and NULL at end of stream. It holds at most n items at a time, plus the block it is reading, and returns them in the order they arrived. For a list, a connection or a function, draw() returns a list rather than a data frame, except with batches = TRUE.

The two paths use different algorithms, so for one seed a stream gives a different sample from a data frame or list holding the same items. Each path on its own gives the same sample for the same seed.

Items in a stream

Each line of a connection is one item, a character string as readLines() returns it, and a header line is an item like any other. To leave a CSV header out of the sample, open the connection, read the header with readLines(con, n = 1) and then draw from the connection, which is read from where the header left off. read.csv(text = c(header, unlist(lines))) turns the sampled lines into a data frame (see the examples). draw() reads a connection in blocks of 10,000 lines, which gives the same sample for a seed as reading it line by line.

A function is called once for each item, and whatever it returns is that item, a data frame included, so a function that returns blocks of rows gives a sample of whole blocks. With batches = TRUE the rows are the items instead: each call returns a data frame of rows, every batch with the same columns in the same order, and draw() returns n of those rows as one data frame, bound with rbind() in the order they arrived. draw() compares only the column names. A column whose type differs between batches, such as one that read.csv() reads as logical in a batch where it is empty, takes the type rbind() gives the sampled rows. Cutting the same rows into batches of other sizes gives the same sample for a seed. Between batches it keeps at most max(2 * n, 1024) rows, some of them already dropped from the sample, besides the batch being read.

What is read

A connection that is not open is opened, read to its end (or to one line past a finite max_items) and closed, as read.csv() does, so it cannot be drawn from twice. A connection that is already open is read from where it stands and left open.

With a finite max_items, draw() reads one item past the cap, because only that read tells a stream of exactly max_items items from a longer one. On an open connection in text mode the line goes back with pushBack(), so the next read starts with it. A connection opened in binary mode ("rb") cannot take a line back, and loses it. A function is called once past the cap and what it returns is dropped; with batches = TRUE, so are the rows of a batch that run past the cap.

References

Vitter, J. S. (1985). Random sampling with a reservoir. ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software, 11, 37–57.

Li, K.-H. (1994). Reservoir-sampling algorithms of time complexity O(n(1 + log(N/n))). ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software, 20, 481–493.

See also

draw()

Other designs: design_bootstrap(), design_certainty(), design_cluster(), design_multistage(), design_simple(), design_spatial(), design_spread(), design_stratified(), design_systematic(), design_temporal(), design_weighted()

Examples

nrow(draw(data.frame(id = 1:1000), design_reservoir(n = 10), seed = 1))
#> [1] 10

# A real stream: a generator that yields 1..50 then stops
i <- 0
gen <- function() {
  i <<- i + 1
  if (i > 50) NULL else i
}
unlist(draw(gen, design_reservoir(n = 5), seed = 1))
#> [1]  4 11 14 32 46

# A CSV file read line by line, with its header left out of the sample
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(data.frame(id = 1:200, value = (1:200) %% 7), path,
          row.names = FALSE)
con <- file(path, "r")
header <- readLines(con, n = 1)
lines <- draw(con, design_reservoir(n = 5), seed = 1)
close(con)
read.csv(text = c(header, unlist(lines)))
#>    id value
#> 1  11     4
#> 2  32     4
#> 3  99     1
#> 4 105     0
#> 5 160     6

# The same file parsed 50 rows at a time, sampling rows: the same five
# rows as above for the same seed
con <- file(path, "r")
header <- readLines(con, n = 1)
next_rows <- function() {
  lines <- readLines(con, n = 50)
  if (length(lines) == 0) NULL else read.csv(text = c(header, lines))
}
draw(next_rows, design_reservoir(n = 5, batches = TRUE), seed = 1)
#>    id value
#> 1  11     4
#> 2  32     4
#> 3  99     1
#> 4 105     0
#> 5 160     6
close(con)
unlink(path)
